notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Physiography refers to the study of physical landforms and relief features of an area.
  • India's present relief is the result of geological structure, plate movements, erosion, deposition and long-term climatic processes.
  • India contains some of the world's youngest fold mountains as well as some of its oldest geological surfaces.
  • Relief varies from high mountains and extensive plains to plateaus, deserts, coastal lowlands and islands.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Physiography → Physical Relief and Landforms

2. Major Physiographic Divisions of India

India is commonly divided into six major physiographic divisions:

  • The Himalayan Mountains.
  • The Northern Plains.
  • The Peninsular Plateau.
  • The Indian Desert.
  • The Coastal Plains.
  • The Islands.
📌 Must-Memorise

India → 6 Major Physiographic Divisions

3. Broad Geological Contrast

India's physiography can broadly be understood through two major geological units:

  • The Peninsular Block.
  • The Himalayan and Northern Plain region.
  • Peninsular India is geologically very old.
  • The Himalayas are geologically young.
  • The Northern Plains are largely depositional.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Oldest Major Landmass → Peninsular Plateau

Young Fold Mountains → Himalayas

Depositional Landform → Northern Plains

4. Peninsular Block
  • The Peninsular Plateau forms one of the oldest and most stable parts of India.
  • It consists mainly of ancient crystalline, igneous and metamorphic rocks.
  • It was once part of the ancient Gondwana landmass.
  • It has been comparatively stable tectonically for a very long period.
  • Weathering and erosion have produced rounded hills, broad valleys and residual mountains.
5. Gondwana Land
  • Gondwana was an ancient southern supercontinent.
  • It included landmasses that later became India, Africa, South America, Australia and Antarctica.
  • The Indian plate later separated and moved northward.
  • Collision with the Eurasian Plate contributed to Himalayan formation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

India's Ancient Geological Association → Gondwana

6. Indian Plate Movement
  • The Indian Plate moved northward after separating from Gondwana.
  • It eventually collided with the Eurasian Plate.
  • This collision began tens of millions of years ago.
  • The collision compressed sediments of the Tethys region and contributed to Himalayan uplift.
  • Plate convergence continues today.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Indian Plate + Eurasian Plate → Himalayas

7. Tethys Sea
  • The Tethys Sea once existed between the Indian and Eurasian landmasses.
  • Sediments accumulated on its floor.
  • Compression and folding of these sediments played a major role in forming the Himalayas.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Tethys Sediments → Himalayan Fold Mountains

8. Himalayan Mountains — Overview
  • The Himalayas form India's northern mountain barrier.
  • They are geologically young fold mountains.
  • They extend in an arc from the Indus region in the west toward the Brahmaputra region in the east.
  • They include some of the world's highest peaks.
  • They strongly influence climate, drainage and settlement.

Detailed Himalayan ranges, divisions, peaks and passes will be covered in Chapter 3.

9. Himalayan Arc
  • The Himalayan system extends for roughly 2,400 km.
  • Its width varies from about 150 km in the east to around 400 km in parts of the west.
  • The mountains form an arc convex toward the south.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Himalayas Length → About 2,400 km

10. Major Parallel Himalayan Ranges

From north to south, the main traditional divisions are:

  • Himadri / Greater Himalaya.
  • Himachal / Lesser Himalaya.
  • Shiwalik / Outer Himalaya.
📌 Must-Memorise

North → South

Himadri → Himachal → Shiwalik

11. Greater Himalaya
  • Greater Himalaya is the northernmost and highest major Himalayan range.
  • It is also called Himadri.
  • It contains many of the highest Himalayan peaks.
  • Permanent snow and glaciers are common.
12. Lesser Himalaya
  • Lesser Himalaya is also called Himachal.
  • It lies south of the Greater Himalaya.
  • It contains many important hill ranges and valleys.
  • Many famous hill stations are located in this belt.
13. Shiwalik Range
  • Shiwalik is the southernmost Himalayan range.
  • It is geologically younger than the inner Himalayan ranges.
  • It consists largely of unconsolidated sediments.
  • Long narrow valleys called duns occur between Shiwaliks and the Lesser Himalayas.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Shiwalik → Outer Himalaya

Dun → Longitudinal Valley

14. Duns

Important examples include:

  • Dehra Dun.
  • Kotli Dun.
  • Patli Dun.
  • Duns are particularly associated with the western Himalayas.
15. Eastern Hills and Purvanchal
  • Beyond the Brahmaputra gorge, the Himalayan system bends southward.
  • These eastern extensions are often called Purvanchal.
  • Major hill groups include Patkai, Naga Hills, Manipur Hills and Mizo/Lushai Hills.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Eastern Himalayan Extension → Purvanchal

16. Northern Plains — Overview
  • The Northern Plains lie south of the Himalayas.
  • They were formed mainly by deposition of alluvium.
  • Major river systems contributing sediments are the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra systems.
  • They form one of the world's largest and most fertile alluvial plains.

Detailed subdivisions will be covered in Chapter 4.

17. Origin of Northern Plains
  • Himalayan rivers carried enormous quantities of sediments.
  • These sediments accumulated in a foreland basin south of the rising Himalayas.
  • Repeated deposition gradually formed the vast Northern Plains.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Northern Plains → River Deposition + Alluvium

18. Importance of Northern Plains

The Northern Plains have:

  • Fertile alluvial soils.
  • Extensive river systems.
  • Flat relief.
  • Dense transport networks.
  • High population concentration.
  • Intensive agriculture.
19. Main Divisions of Northern Plains

Broadly, the plains include:

  • Punjab Plain.
  • Ganga Plain.
  • Brahmaputra Plain.
📌 Must-Memorise

Northern Plains → Punjab + Ganga + Brahmaputra

20. Bhabar
  • Bhabar is a narrow belt along the foothills of the Shiwaliks.
  • Rivers deposit coarse pebbles and gravels here.
  • Streams often disappear into the porous deposits.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bhabar → Pebbles + Porous Belt + Streams Disappear

21. Terai
  • Terai lies south of the Bhabar.
  • Underground streams re-emerge in this region.
  • It is generally marshy and waterlogged.
  • Historically, it had dense forests.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Terai → Marshy + Streams Re-emerge

22. Bhangar
  • Bhangar is older alluvium.
  • It generally lies above active floodplains.
  • It may contain calcareous nodules called kankar.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bhangar → Older Alluvium

23. Khadar
  • Khadar is newer alluvium.
  • It is deposited in active floodplains.
  • It is renewed by periodic floods.
  • It is generally highly fertile.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bhangar → Old Alluvium

Khadar → New Alluvium

24. Peninsular Plateau — Overview
  • The Peninsular Plateau lies south of the Northern Plains.
  • It is a tableland composed largely of ancient crystalline rocks.
  • It is triangular in broad outline.
  • It is one of the oldest physiographic regions of India.

Detailed divisions will be covered in Chapter 5.

25. General Slope of Peninsular Plateau
  • Much of the Peninsular Plateau slopes gently eastward.
  • Therefore, many major peninsular rivers flow eastward toward the Bay of Bengal.
  • Some important rivers such as Narmada and Tapi flow westward.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Peninsular General Slope → Eastward

26. Major Peninsular Plateau Divisions

Broad divisions include:

  • Central Highlands.
  • Deccan Plateau.

The Narmada River region is often treated as an important dividing zone between these two broad sections.

27. Central Highlands

The Central Highlands include areas associated with:

  • Malwa Plateau.
  • Bundelkhand.
  • Baghelkhand.
  • Chotanagpur Plateau.
  • They generally lie north of the Narmada.
28. Deccan Plateau
  • Deccan Plateau lies mainly south of the Narmada.
  • It has a roughly triangular shape.
  • Western Ghats form its western margin.
  • Eastern Ghats form a more discontinuous eastern margin.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Deccan Plateau → South of Narmada

29. Western Ghats
  • Western Ghats run roughly parallel to India's western coast.
  • They form a more continuous escarpment than the Eastern Ghats.
  • They are generally higher than the Eastern Ghats.
  • They strongly influence southwest monsoon rainfall.

Detailed ranges and peaks will be covered later.

30. Eastern Ghats
  • Eastern Ghats run along parts of India's eastern side.
  • They are discontinuous.
  • Major rivers cut across them while flowing toward the Bay of Bengal.
  • They are generally lower than the Western Ghats.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Western Ghats → More continuous

Eastern Ghats → More discontinuous

31. Meeting of Eastern and Western Ghats
  • The Eastern and Western Ghats meet in the Nilgiri Hills.
  • The Nilgiris lie around the junction of Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Karnataka.
📌 Must-Memorise

Eastern Ghats + Western Ghats → Nilgiri Hills

32. Tamil Nadu Physiographic Link

Tamil Nadu contains parts of:

  • Eastern Ghats.
  • Western Ghats.
  • Nilgiri Hills.
  • Coastal plains.
  • Interior plateaus and uplands.

This gives Tamil Nadu substantial relief diversity.

33. Indian Desert — Overview
  • The Indian Desert lies mainly west of the Aravalli Hills.
  • It is commonly called the Thar Desert.
  • It occurs primarily in Rajasthan.
  • It extends into adjoining Gujarat and across the international boundary into Pakistan.

Detailed desert landforms will be treated in Chapter 6.

34. Thar Desert
  • Thar is characterised by low rainfall.
  • Sandy plains and sand dunes are common.
  • Drainage is sparse and often seasonal.
  • Luni is the most important river system of the Indian desert region.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Indian Desert → Thar

Major River → Luni

35. Aravalli Range
  • Aravalli is one of India's oldest fold-mountain systems.
  • It extends broadly from Gujarat through Rajasthan toward Delhi.
  • It forms an important physiographic boundary between the desert and more eastern regions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

One of India's Oldest Mountain Systems → Aravalli

36. Coastal Plains — Overview

India has two major coastal-plain systems:

  • Western Coastal Plain.
  • Eastern Coastal Plain.

They differ greatly in width, relief, river mouths and coastal features.

37. Western Coastal Plain
  • Western Coastal Plain lies between the Western Ghats and Arabian Sea.
  • It is generally narrow.
  • It contains many estuaries.
  • Major regional divisions traditionally include Konkan, Kannad/Kanara and Malabar coasts.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Western Coastal Plain → Narrow + Estuaries

38. Eastern Coastal Plain
  • Eastern Coastal Plain lies between the Eastern Ghats and Bay of Bengal.
  • It is generally broader than the Western Coastal Plain.
  • Major east-flowing rivers have built extensive deltas.
  • Regional divisions include Northern Circars and Coromandel Coast.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Eastern Coastal Plain → Broad + Deltas

39. Western vs Eastern Coast

Western coast:

  • Narrow.
  • More estuaries.
  • Western Ghats close to sea.

Eastern coast:

  • Wider.
  • Large deltas.
  • Major rivers cross Eastern Ghats.
📌 Must-Memorise

West → Estuaries

East → Deltas

40. Konkan Coast
  • Konkan Coast lies along parts of Maharashtra and Goa.
  • It forms the northern section of the western coastal plain in standard textbook classification.
41. Kanara/Kannad Coast
  • Kanara or Karnataka Coast lies mainly along Karnataka.
  • It forms the middle section of the western coastal plain.
42. Malabar Coast
  • Malabar Coast lies mainly along Kerala.
  • Lagoons and backwaters are important features.
  • Kerala's backwaters are locally called kayals.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Malabar → Kerala → Backwaters

43. Northern Circars
  • Northern Circars form part of the eastern coastal plain.
  • They are associated mainly with Andhra Pradesh and adjoining Odisha coastal sectors in traditional geography.
44. Coromandel Coast
  • Coromandel Coast lies along southeastern India.
  • Much of Tamil Nadu's eastern coastline forms part of the Coromandel Coast.
  • It faces the Bay of Bengal.
  • It receives a significant share of rainfall from the northeast monsoon.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Tamil Nadu East Coast → Coromandel Coast

45. Deltas of Eastern Coast

Major river deltas include:

  • Mahanadi.
  • Godavari.
  • Krishna.
  • Kaveri.
📌 Must-Memorise

Major East-Coast Deltas → Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri

46. Estuaries of Western Coast

Important west-flowing rivers forming estuarine mouths include:

  • Narmada.
  • Tapi.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Narmada + Tapi → Estuaries

47. Islands of India — Overview

India has two major island groups:

  • Lakshadweep in the Arabian Sea.
  • Andaman and Nicobar Islands in the Bay of Bengal/Andaman Sea region.

Detailed island formation and relief will be covered in Chapter 6.

48. Lakshadweep — Physiographic Character
  • Lakshadweep consists mainly of coral islands.
  • Many islands are associated with atolls and reefs.
  • They are low-lying.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lakshadweep → Coral Origin

49. Andaman and Nicobar — Physiographic Character
  • Andaman and Nicobar Islands are largely related to submerged mountain chains and tectonic island arcs.
  • They are more elevated and rugged than Lakshadweep.
  • Some islands are volcanic.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

A&N → Tectonic/Volcanic Island Arc

Lakshadweep → Coral Islands

50. Barren Island
  • Barren Island lies in the Andaman Sea region.
  • It contains India's only confirmed active volcano.
📌 Must-Memorise

India's Active Volcano → Barren Island

51. Narcondam
  • Narcondam is a volcanic island in the Andaman region.
  • It is generally considered dormant/extinct in standard textbook geography rather than currently active.
52. Relief and Drainage Relationship
  • India's relief controls river direction and drainage patterns.
  • Himalayan rivers originate in high mountains and generally have perennial flow.
  • Peninsular rivers flow across an older plateau surface.
  • Western and eastern coastal relief influences whether rivers form estuaries or deltas.
53. Relief and Climate

Major physiographic controls on climate include:

  • Himalayas blocking cold Central Asian winds.
  • Western Ghats causing orographic rainfall.
  • Plateau interiors experiencing more continental conditions.
  • Coastal plains experiencing maritime influence.

Detailed climate is covered later.

54. Himalayas as Climatic Barrier
  • Himalayas obstruct cold winds from Central Asia.
  • They force moisture-bearing monsoon winds to rise.
  • They strongly influence rainfall distribution over northern India.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Himalayas → Climatic Barrier

55. Western Ghats and Rainfall
  • Southwest monsoon winds strike the western slopes of the Western Ghats.
  • Orographic uplift causes heavy rainfall on the windward side.
  • Rain-shadow conditions occur east of the Ghats in many areas.
56. Physiography and Agriculture
  • Northern Plains support intensive agriculture because of fertile alluvial soils and flat terrain.
  • Plateau regions contain diverse soils and mineral resources.
  • Coastal plains support rice, coconut and other crops.
  • Mountain regions support terrace farming and horticulture.
57. Physiography and Population
  • Flat fertile plains have high population densities.
  • Rugged mountain regions generally have lower densities.
  • Coastal plains support many major cities and ports.
  • Plateau areas contain major mining and industrial centres.
58. Physiography and Transport
  • Northern Plains favour road and railway construction.
  • Mountain terrain makes transport more difficult.
  • Plateaus require bridges, cuttings and gradients.
  • Coastal plains provide sites for ports and coastal transport.
59. Physiography and Minerals
  • Peninsular Plateau contains a large share of India's mineral wealth.
  • Ancient rocks host coal, iron ore, manganese, bauxite and other minerals.
  • The Chotanagpur Plateau is particularly mineral-rich.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mineral Heartland → Peninsular Plateau / Chotanagpur Region

60. Physiography and Hydroelectric Power
  • Mountainous regions provide steep gradients suitable for hydropower.
  • Himalayan rivers have large flow volumes.
  • Western Ghats also provide important hydropower sites.
61. Physiography and Natural Hazards

Different physiographic regions face different hazards:

  • Himalayas → Earthquakes, landslides, avalanches.
  • Northern Plains → Floods.
  • Desert → Drought and sand movement.
  • Coastal Plains → Cyclones and storm surges.
  • Islands → Tsunami and coastal hazards.
62. Geological Stability of Peninsular India
  • Peninsular India is generally more stable than the Himalayan region.
  • However, it is not completely free from earthquakes.
  • Intraplate earthquakes can occur.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Peninsular India → Stable, not earthquake-free.

63. Himalayan Tectonic Activity
  • Himalayas lie in an active plate-collision zone.
  • Continuing convergence causes crustal deformation.
  • Therefore, the Himalayan belt is highly earthquake-prone.
64. India's Relief Extremes

India includes:

  • Extremely high mountains.
  • Extensive low alluvial plains.
  • Ancient plateaus.
  • Arid desert.
  • Low coastal plains.
  • Coral and volcanic islands.

This makes India one of the world's most physiographically diverse countries.

65. Young Fold Mountains vs Old Fold Mountains
  • Himalayas are young fold mountains.
  • Aravallis are among the oldest fold-mountain systems.
  • The contrast is frequently tested.
📌 Must-Memorise

Young Fold → Himalayas

Old Fold → Aravallis

66. Depositional vs Erosional Landscapes

Depositional landforms dominate:

  • Northern Plains.
  • Major river deltas.

Erosional and structural landforms dominate much of:

  • Peninsular Plateau.
  • Mountain areas.
67. Alluvial Plains
  • Alluvial plains form from sediments deposited by rivers.
  • Northern Plains are India's largest continuous alluvial region.
  • Eastern coastal deltas are also strongly alluvial.
68. Plateau
  • A plateau is an elevated relatively flat or rolling land surface.
  • Peninsular India is a large plateau region.
  • Plateaus can be dissected by rivers and erosion.
69. Coastal Plain
  • Coastal plains are low-lying regions adjoining the sea.
  • India's eastern coastal plain is generally broader.
  • Western coastal plain is generally narrower.
70. Island
  • An island is land surrounded by water.
  • India's islands differ in geological origin.
  • Lakshadweep is coral.
  • Andaman-Nicobar is largely tectonic and volcanic in origin.
71. Physiographic Sequence from North to South

A simplified north-to-south sequence is:

Himalayas → Northern Plains → Peninsular Plateau → Coastal Plains → Indian Ocean/Islands

📌 TNPSC Map Memory

North → Mountains

Centre-North → Plains

South → Plateau

Margins → Coasts

72. Physiographic Sequence in Western India

Broad westward sequence in parts of India:

Aravalli region → Thar Desert → Gujarat plains/coast → Arabian Sea

73. Physiographic Sequence in Southern India

In southern peninsular India:

Western Coastal Plain → Western Ghats → Interior Plateau → Eastern Ghats → Eastern Coastal Plain

📌 Must-Memorise

West to East in South India:

Arabian Sea → Western Coastal Plain → Western Ghats → Plateau → Eastern Ghats → Eastern Coastal Plain → Bay of Bengal

74. Tamil Nadu — Major Physiographic Units

Tamil Nadu broadly includes:

  • Western Ghats along the western side.
  • Eastern Ghats in northern and interior sectors.
  • Plateau and upland surfaces.
  • River valleys.
  • Eastern coastal plains.
  • Coromandel Coast.
  • Kanyakumari coastal region.
75. Nilgiri Hills
  • Nilgiri Hills lie where the Western and Eastern Ghats converge.
  • They occupy parts of northwestern Tamil Nadu.
  • They form an important highland region of southern India.

Detailed peaks will be covered in the Peninsular Plateau chapter.

76. Palghat Gap — Overview Link
  • Palghat Gap is an important break in the Western Ghats.
  • It lies between the Nilgiri Hills and Anaimalai Hills.
  • It connects Kerala with Tamil Nadu.
  • It is important for transport and wind movement.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Palghat Gap → Kerala–Tamil Nadu Corridor

77. Shencottah Gap
  • Shencottah or Shenkottai Gap is another important passage through the southern Western Ghats.
  • It links parts of Tamil Nadu and Kerala.
78. Coromandel Plain
  • Tamil Nadu contains much of the Coromandel coastal plain.
  • The Kaveri delta forms one of its major fertile sections.
  • Coastal topography influences agriculture, settlements and cyclone exposure.
79. Kaveri Delta
  • Kaveri forms an important delta in Tamil Nadu.
  • It lies within the eastern coastal plain.
  • It is one of Tamil Nadu's most important agricultural regions.

Detailed river facts belong to the river chapter.

80. Physical Division — Major Character Summary

Himalayas:

  • Young.
  • Fold mountains.
  • High relief.

Northern Plains:

  • Depositional.
  • Alluvial.
  • Flat.

Peninsular Plateau:

  • Ancient.
  • Crystalline.
  • Mineral-rich.

Indian Desert:

  • Arid.
  • Sandy.
  • Sparse drainage.

Coastal Plains:

  • Low-lying.
  • West narrow, east broad.

Islands:

  • Coral and tectonic/volcanic origins.
81. Physiographic Comparison — Himalayas vs Peninsular Plateau

Himalayas:

  • Geologically young.
  • Folded.
  • High and rugged.
  • Tectonically active.
  • Deep gorges and glaciers.

Peninsular Plateau:

  • Geologically ancient.
  • Stable block.
  • Lower and more eroded.
  • Broad valleys and rounded hills.
  • Rich in minerals.
82. Northern Plains vs Peninsular Plateau

Northern Plains:

  • Young depositional surface.
  • Mostly alluvium.
  • Flat.
  • Dense population.
  • Intensive agriculture.

Peninsular Plateau:

  • Ancient hard-rock surface.
  • Uneven relief.
  • Rich in minerals.
  • Numerous plateaus and hills.
83. Western vs Eastern Coastal Plains

Western:

  • Narrow.
  • Western Ghats close to coast.
  • Estuaries common.
  • Backwaters especially in Kerala.

Eastern:

  • Broad.
  • Major deltas.
  • Larger coastal plains.
  • More exposed to Bay of Bengal cyclones.
84. Western Ghats vs Eastern Ghats

Western Ghats:

  • Higher.
  • More continuous.
  • Strong escarpment.
  • Major climatic barrier.

Eastern Ghats:

  • Lower.
  • Discontinuous.
  • Cut by major rivers.
  • Approach coast less continuously.
85. Northern Mountain Barrier and Indian Identity
  • Himalayas form a distinct northern physiographic boundary.
  • Peninsular seas form southern and lateral maritime boundaries.
  • Together they contribute to the geographical unity of the Indian subcontinent.

Students should locate:

  • Himalayas.
  • Shiwaliks.
  • Northern Plains.
  • Punjab Plain.
  • Ganga Plain.
  • Brahmaputra Plain.

  • Western Ghats.
  • Eastern Ghats.
  • Nilgiris.
  • Western Coastal Plain.
  • Eastern Coastal Plain.
  • Lakshadweep.
  • Andaman and Nicobar.
87. TNPSC High-Yield Pairings
  • Young fold mountains → Himalayas.
  • Old fold mountains → Aravallis.
  • Alluvial plain → Northern Plains.
  • Old crystalline block → Peninsular Plateau.
  • Indian desert → Thar.
  • Western coastal plain → Narrow.
  • Eastern coastal plain → Broad.
  • Arabian Sea islands → Lakshadweep.
  • Bay of Bengal island group → Andaman and Nicobar.
  • Active volcano → Barren Island.
  • Eastern + Western Ghats → Nilgiris.
  • Tamil Nadu east coast → Coromandel.
88. Common Map Traps
  • Aravalli lies west/northwest of the main Peninsular Plateau region.
  • Western Ghats are not directly on the shoreline everywhere; a narrow coastal plain lies between them and the sea.
  • Eastern Ghats are not continuous.
  • Thar lies mainly west of Aravalli.
  • Chotanagpur lies in eastern Peninsular India.
  • Nilgiris are not part of the Himalayas.
  • Lakshadweep is west of India.
  • Andaman and Nicobar are east/southeast of mainland India.

  • Ancient sea associated with Himalayan formation? → Tethys Sea.
  • Approximate Himalayan length? → About 2,400 km.
  • Three major Himalayan ranges from north to south? → Himadri, Himachal and Shiwalik.
  • Highest major Himalayan range? → Himadri/Greater Himalaya.
  • Outer Himalaya? → Shiwalik.
  • Longitudinal valleys associated with Shiwaliks? → Duns.
  • Example? → Dehra Dun.
  • Eastern Himalayan hills collectively called? → Purvanchal.
  • Major Purvanchal hills? → Patkai, Naga, Manipur and Mizo hills.
  • Northern Plains formed mainly by? → River-borne alluvium.
  • Three main river systems forming Northern Plains? → Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra.
  • Three broad divisions of Northern Plains? → Punjab, Ganga and Brahmaputra plains.
  • Bhabar consists mainly of? → Pebbles and coarse sediments.
  • What happens to streams in Bhabar? → They often disappear underground.
  • Region south of Bhabar? → Terai.
  • Terai characteristic? → Marshy and waterlogged.
  • Older alluvium? → Bhangar.
  • Newer alluvium? → Khadar.
  • Calcareous nodules in Bhangar called? → Kankar.
  • Oldest major physiographic division? → Peninsular Plateau.
  • General slope of Peninsular Plateau? → Eastward.
  • Two broad plateau divisions? → Central Highlands and Deccan Plateau.
  • Central Highlands lie mainly? → North of Narmada.
  • Deccan Plateau lies mainly? → South of Narmada.
  • Which Ghats are more continuous? → Western Ghats.
  • Which Ghats are more discontinuous? → Eastern Ghats.
  • Which Ghats are generally higher? → Western Ghats.
  • Eastern and Western Ghats meet at? → Nilgiri Hills.
  • Main desert of India? → Thar Desert.
  • Thar Desert lies mainly in? → Rajasthan.
  • Mountain range east of much of Thar? → Aravalli.
  • One of India's oldest fold mountains? → Aravalli.
  • Major river of Indian Desert? → Luni.
  • Two main coastal plains? → Western and Eastern Coastal Plains.
  • Which coastal plain is narrower? → Western Coastal Plain.
  • Which is broader? → Eastern Coastal Plain.
  • Which coast has large river deltas? → Eastern coast.
  • Which coast commonly has estuaries? → Western coast.
  • Three traditional western coastal divisions? → Konkan, Kanara/Kannad and Malabar.
  • Malabar Coast associated with? → Kerala.
  • Kerala backwaters called? → Kayals.
  • Two major eastern coastal divisions? → Northern Circars and Coromandel Coast.
  • Coromandel Coast associated mainly with? → Tamil Nadu.
  • Major eastern deltas? → Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri.
  • Two major rivers forming estuaries on western side? → Narmada and Tapi.
  • Island group in Arabian Sea? → Lakshadweep.
  • Lakshadweep geological origin? → Coral.
  • Island group east of mainland? → Andaman and Nicobar.
  • Andaman-Nicobar origin broadly? → Tectonic island arc with volcanic features.
  • India's active volcano? → Barren Island.
  • Where is Barren Island? → Andaman Sea region.
  • Main climatic barrier of northern India? → Himalayas.
  • Major orographic barrier of western peninsular India? → Western Ghats.
  • Major mineral-rich physiographic division? → Peninsular Plateau.
  • Chotanagpur Plateau known for? → Mineral wealth.
  • Which physiographic region has highest population concentration? → Northern Plains.
  • Which physiographic region is most suitable for extensive road and railway construction? → Northern Plains.
  • Which region is most earthquake-prone? → Himalayan belt.
  • Is Peninsular India completely free from earthquakes? → No.
  • Major Tamil Nadu physiographic associations? → Western Ghats, Eastern Ghats, Nilgiris, interior plateau and eastern coastal plain.
  • Important gap connecting Kerala and Tamil Nadu? → Palghat Gap.
  • Palghat Gap lies between? → Nilgiri and Anaimalai hills.
  • Important Tamil Nadu coastal plain? → Coromandel Coast.
  • Kaveri delta belongs to which physiographic region? → Eastern Coastal Plain.
